I am a social scientist working on international political economy, global health and development, and African politics. I am `r site$title` in the `r site$department$name` at `r site$institution$name`, where I have taught since 2017, and `r aff$role` at the `r aff$organisation`. Before Royal Holloway, I was a Lecturer in Sociology at the University of Waikato in New Zealand and, before that, a Research Associate in Sociology at the University of Cambridge, where I took my PhD.

Beyond the research described below, I write on African politics: on elections in Kenya, Rwanda, and Burundi, on ethnicity and the military in Kenya, and on conflict in the Sahel.

## Research

My research examines how the global economy is governed, and what that means for people's health and social protection, for the climate, and for countries in crisis. Its main subjects are international financial institutions, whose loans and advice shape economic policy across much of the world, and much of it rests on original data built from their own documents. It follows three strands.

### Global economic governance, health, and social protection

What do economic policies devised at the global level do to societies and states? With Alexandros Kentikelenis and other colleagues, I have built a dataset of the policy conditions attached to IMF loans over four decades, drawn from the IMF's own archives. With it, we study how austerity and market reforms affect health systems and child health, social protection, poverty, and inequality, and how they reshape states and politics: administrative capacity, taxation, labour rights, corruption, and protest. Our book *A Thousand Cuts* (Oxford University Press, 2023) brings this work together. It finds that although the content of IMF-mandated austerity has changed, the IMF still places a high burden of reform on its borrowers, and that these reforms reduce the availability of social services, widen income inequality, and harm population health. More recent work follows the wave of austerity that came after the Covid-19 pandemic, and what it means for public health. The data are public on the [`r site$imf_monitor$name`](`r site$imf_monitor$url`), which I curate. A Philip Leverhulme Prize, for 2027–28, will support the next stage of this work, on the social consequences of global economic governance.

### Global economic governance and the climate crisis

How are the institutions that govern the global economy responding to climate change? I study how the green transition has entered the work of international financial institutions, in their economic surveillance, lending, and technical assistance, and how far practice matches their public commitments. Our book *Greening the International Monetary Fund* (Cambridge University Press, 2025) finds that green transition objectives have become embedded in the IMF's activities in varied and at times contradictory ways. A [series of reports](../policy/index.qmd) for Recourse Foundation, since 2021, follows each of these activities in turn.

```{r}
           "FNST6FDY"))  # Green rhetoric, grey reality, Recourse Foundation (2025)
```

### Crisis finance and the global financial safety net

Who gets help when a crisis hits, and on what terms? This strand studies the global financial safety net: the IMF resources, regional financing arrangements, and central bank swap lines that countries turn to in a crisis. It asks how the safety net responded to Covid-19, how far it reaches developing countries, and how well its structure can absorb global shocks. It also examines the terms on which help comes: how much room loan conditions leave governments to set their own policies, whether reform programmes can be carried out as designed, and what follows when they are not.

## Policy engagement

Alongside my academic research, I undertake commissioned research and advisory work for international organisations, governments, and civil society, including the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ), Oxfam International, Recourse Foundation, and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF). I have presented my research at the IMF, UNICEF, and Oxfam America, and my work is cited in documents of the IMF and its Independent Evaluation Office, the United Nations General Assembly and Human Rights Council, the World Health Organization, the International Labour Organization, and the European Central Bank, among others. My policy reports are listed on [Policy & Advisory](../policy/index.qmd).

## Service

I have sat on the Editorial Board of *Globalization & Health* since 2026, and am Guest Editor of a special issue of the journal in 2026–27. I have reviewed for more than 40 journals, among them the *American Journal of Sociology*, the *American Political Science Review*, the *Review of International Political Economy*, the *Review of International Organizations*, *Social Science & Medicine*, and *World Development*; for book publishers, among them Cambridge University Press, Oxford University Press, and Routledge; and for the Swiss National Science Foundation and the Wellcome Trust.

At Royal Holloway, I was Director of Undergraduate Education in the School of Law and Social Sciences from 2022 to 2026. In the department, I have been Director of Impact (2021–22), Director of Research (2020–21), Director of External Engagement (2019–20), and Co-Director of the Global Politics and Development Centre (2019–21).
